cover.alt: The sorting pen from above on réttir day: a round stone-walled pen in the middle full of white, grey and black sheep, small owners' pens around it like petals, farmers dragging sheep into them, children sitting on the wall.
cover.art_brief: Late September 1874, overcast autumn day on the flat river meadow below the farms of Jökuldalur, brown-and-rust hills behind. High three-quarter view from above of a round communal sorting pen (rétt) of dry stone and turf: the large central pen (almenningur) packed with white, grey and black Icelandic sheep; around its outer wall, like petals of a flower, about ten small owners' pens (dilkar), each opening into the centre by a gap. Farmers in plain homespun drag sheep by the horns from the centre towards their own pens; one big white ram pulls a red-bearded man (Óli) along. Children sit on the top of the wall: among them a small girl in a red dress and black tasselled skotthúfa (Ásta, 6) and two boys (Siggi, 11, sandy hair, brown jumper; Ketill, 12, black hair under a dark knitted cap). Horses tethered outside, dogs at the gaps. Established farm ink-and-watercolour style. No text, letters or numerals.

grammar.note_en:
A case is a form of a noun, name, adjective or pronoun that shows its job in the sentence. The nominative (nf., nefnifall) is the form you already know: the subject, the person or thing that does something or that the sentence is about. The accusative (þf., þolfall) is new: it is the object, the person or thing that something is done to. In this chapter the object is what someone owns, sees, finds, takes, pulls, examines, recognises, wants or buys.

The chapter's joke shows why the endings matter. Óli dregur ekki hrútinn: hrúturinn dregur Óla! (s028) means "Óli isn't pulling the ram: the ram is pulling Óli!" In the first half Óli is the subject and hrútinn the object; in the second half hrúturinn is the subject and Óla the object. Icelandic does not need the subject to come first, because the endings say who does what: Nú dregur hrúturinn Óla! (s027), "Now the ram is pulling Óli!" After nú the verb comes second and the subject follows it, but hrúturinn is still the subject and Óla still the object.

Nouns with the article ("the"). The article is an ending, and it changes for the accusative too:
- feminine: kindin → kindina. En kindin stendur ("But the ewe stands still"); Pabbi á kindina! (s019, "Dad owns the ewe!"). The same -ina is in bókina: Afi tekur bókina (s064, "Grandad takes the book").
- masculine: hrúturinn → hrútinn. The nominative is hrút-ur-inn; the accusative drops the -ur: hrút-inn. En hrúturinn kemur ekki (s026, "But the ram doesn't come"); Óli tekur hrútinn (s025, "Óli takes hold of the ram").
- neuter: lambið → lambið, no change. Kindin og lambið standa á túninu (s002, "The ewe and the lamb stand on the home field"); Siggi skoðar lambið (s003, "Siggi looks the lamb over"). Markið (the earmark) is the same: Hann skoðar markið (s004, "He examines the earmark"). In neuter words subject and object look alike, so the verb and the sense tell you which is which.
- feminine plural: kindurnar → kindurnar, no change. Kindurnar jarma (s015, "The sheep bleat"); Bjarni skoðar kindurnar (s017, "Bjarni looks over the sheep").
Without the article, dilkur → dilk loses its nominative -ur (Bjarni á dilk, s014, "Bjarni has a pen"), and hrútur → hrút does the same (Nú sér Ásta stóran hrút, s022, "Now Ásta sees a big ram"). Masculine nouns have other patterns too, so learn their forms as they come. Kind and lamb do not change: Nú á Siggi lamb (s054, "Now Siggi owns a lamb").

Adjectives agree with their noun in case as well. Nú finnur hann gráa kind (s018) is "Now he finds a grey ewe": grá kind as subject, gráa kind as object. Nú sér Ásta stóran hrút (s022) is "Now Ásta sees a big ram": stór hrútur as subject, stóran hrút as object. In Bjarni skoðar kindurnar: hvítar, svartar og gráar (s017, "Bjarni looks over the sheep: white, black and grey") the feminine plural accusative colours look exactly like the nominative.

Names change too. Óli → Óla, Siggi → Sigga, Ketill → Ketil: Afi skilur Sigga (s059, "Grandad understands Siggi"); Lambið … vill ekki Sigga, og það vill ekki Ketil (s042, "The lamb doesn't want Siggi, and it doesn't want Ketill"). Jón stays Jón.

Pronouns. Hún becomes hana: Bjarni dregur hana (s020, "Bjarni pulls her", the ewe); Hann skoðar hana (s065, "He looks at it", the book, because bók is feminine). Hann stays hann: Bjarni á hann (s024, "Bjarni owns him", the ram). Það stays það: Ketill skoðar það líka (s037, "Ketill looks at it too"). In the plural, þeir becomes þá, þær stays þær and þau stays þau: Jón og Ketill fara, og nú sér Siggi þá ekki (s053, "Jón and Ketill leave, and now Siggi can't see them"); Jón finnur kindur líka, og Ketill dregur þær í dilkinn (s021, "Jón finds ewes too, and Ketill pulls them into the pen"); Kindin og lambið eru þar, og Siggi sér þau (s055, "The ewe and the lamb are there, and Siggi sees them"). As in Kafli 1, the pronoun follows the noun's gender, so an animal or a thing can be "her" or "him" in Icelandic where English says "it".

Questions. Hver? asks for the subject: Hver á hrútinn? (s023, "Who owns the ram?"). Hvern? asks for a masculine object: Hvern vill lambið? Sigga eða Ketil? (s041, "Whom does the lamb want? Siggi or Ketill?"); the lamb is the subject, and the answer is an accusative: … það vill kindina! (s042, "… it wants the ewe!"). Hvað? is "what?" and looks the same as subject and object: Hvað gerir Bjarni nú? (s043, "What will Bjarni do now?").

Eiga "to own" takes an accusative object. Its present á ("owns") looks like the á of á túninu ("on the home field"), but it is a verb: Hver á þetta lamb? (s033, "Who owns this lamb?"); Nú á Siggi lambið (s050, "Now Siggi owns the lamb"). Þetta lamb shows þessi "this" in the neuter accusative, identical to the nominative.

One more accusative. The preposition um takes the accusative: Um kvöldið er féð á túninu (s055, "In the evening the sheep are on the home field"); kvöldið looks the same as the nominative because it is neuter. Learn um kvöldið as "in the evening".

Í dilkinn (s020, s021, s029, s031) means "into the pen". Learn this whole expression for now; Kafli 6 explains the pattern.

introductions.how: Title and question Hvað eru réttir?; the adjacent explanation contrasts göngur up on the heath with réttir down below (s011); rétt named beside its actual SVG (s013).
Contrast: the rétt is big, the dilkar small; Bjarni and Jón each own one. Actual labelled sorting-pen SVG precedes the noun.
Ownership statement raises Siggi’s question; Óli defines the district as the farms together at s046. First token lacks an immediate definition: explicit review question retained.
Known-word margin definition: fé: kindur og lömb. Singular collective illustrated by Féð kemur.
Contrast with kind in a margin gloss; large white animal reverses the pulling at s025–s029. Raster vignette is only planned; narrow ewe/ram meaning needs review.
Action sequence: Óli takes the ram and pulls it; repeated with the book passing from Bjarni to afi at s064.
Example gloss Hvar? … Hér! and Bjarni picking out a grey ewe from the sheep.
Example gloss þekkir markið: «Bjarni!»; ownership immediately follows at s019.
Contrast with taking it without payment; actual coin-comparison SVG at the same segment supplies the transaction.
The ewe stands still, Bjarni pulls her, and then she goes into the pen. Reversal with Óli and the ram at s027–s028.
Both boys call the lamb at s038–s039; báðir vilja lambið followed by Ásta asking whom the lamb wants and its preference for the ewe.
Siggi asks Hver er það? and does not understand; Óli answers at s046. Later afi understands Siggi and Bjarni understands afi’s hint.
Known-word definition skoðar: sér hér, sér þar; looking at the lamb and then its mark.
Example gloss: Jón? Nei. Bjarni? Nei. Later ekkert is linked to enginn and Ketill’s silence.
Example gloss báðir: Siggi og Ketill, after their two identical calls.
Question alternatives: Pabbi eða Jón?; margin example Pabbi? Jón?
Siggi and Ketill, known companions from the rescue, run together; later called góðir vinir.
Óli’s positive appraisal góðir vinir; Bjarni and afi each say Gott lamb. Meaning support is contextual rather than a synonym; reviewer asked to assess it.
Known colours contrasted in margin: not white, not black; then Bjarni finds a grey ewe. Planned vignette not counted as support.
Actual SVG contrasts many coins for a horse and few for the lamb, labelled ódýrt.
Margin definition bændurnir gera það aftur og aftur; Siggi reacts to the old custom.
Known-word repeated-action definition skoðar … og skoðar; book later comes back.
Two boys running together; contrast with einn, then ewe and lamb go together at s031.
Contrast margir ↔ einn; a single farmer among many. At s051 contrast einn ↔ saman makes the alone sense explicit.
Contrast sumar ↔ haust; cold morning and seasonal sorting day.
Known-word time gloss um kvöldið: nú er kvöld.
Whole direction chunk: ewe stands still, is pulled, then goes into the pen; the actual labelled pen SVG at s013 supplies the destination.
First object lambið (s003); first visibly different object gráa kind (s018) then kindin → kindina form gloss (s019). The ram reverses subject and object in the joke at s028.

words_with_history.title: Orð með sögu
text: Bjarni á mark, og Jón á mark. Margir bændur eiga mark.
Bjarni skoðar markið og þekkir það. „Pabbi á kindina!“ segir Siggi.
En lambið hefur skrítið mark, og enginn þekkir það.
words_with_history.note_en: Every farm cut its own pattern of notches, slits and holes into its sheep's ears. The marks were recorded in a register, the markaskrá, so that a stray could be traced at the réttir. Icelandic mark is the same word as English mark.

pronunciation_note.rule: ll after a vowel: [tl]; rn: [tn], rl: [tl]. Learn these patterns in the examples; they are not exceptionless rules.

notes: Learner-load ledger: about 555 running story tokens (see metrics); 27 planned lexemes = 26 single lexemes + 1 direction chunk (í dilkinn). No open-slot additions. Eiga already exists from Kafli 3, so no duplicate delta entry. Prior-token coverage 84.23%; new/aided share 15.77% (85 of 539 tokens), from the chapter gate. New inflected forms include kindina, hrútinn, bókina; object hana/hann/það; Óla/Sigga/Ketil; hvern; gráa and the unchanged feminine-plural accusatives in s017; kvöldið after um; ekkert. Homographs are not separate new lexemes.

New-form load is concentrated at s017–s020 (plural colours, gráa kind, recognition, kindina, dregur hana, í dilkinn) and s040–s046 (báðir vilja, hvern and name objects, hreppur/siður/skilur). The introductory table records the actual routes, including their limitations, not imagined support from planned pictures. First visible accusative contrast arrives at s018–s019, within the first third; the ram joke and the lamb’s preference turn the target into consequences.

Incidental strong/irregular present forms and plural forms are supplied context, never answers in conjugation drills. Báðir and the numerals are not blanked or placed in paradigms. After the independent review (2026-11-07) the story was given the plural object pronouns in consequential places — þær (s021, Ketill helping his father pen their ewes), þá (s053, Jón and Ketill gone from sight), þau (s055, the ewe and lamb at home) — and a masculine accusative adjective, stóran hrút (s022); all are tabulated and practised (x1-2-5, a3). Þau is used solely as the already known subject (G03 recall). Adjective tables show only the feminine accusatives actually read, not the plan’s unencountered masculine adjective paradigm.

Length and three-use quotas are advisory: keep the fixed story rather than pad it. The recall carrier is only partly realised: dry plentiful hay and the sheep home are stated at s063; there is no full present-tense recap of haycock/rain or the foggy round-up. Recycle focus passes at 22/26 (84.6%); is-upp, is-hlada, is-stelpa and is-gras are carried forward. Record this omission instead of silently inventing a completed carrier.

Two margin vignettes rather than the checker’s suggested four to ten are deliberate; both genuine scenes have planned pictures and two actual SVGs provide exact support. No extra decorative vignette was added to satisfy an advisory count. All audio remains suspended.

Grammar note exceeds the short-note warning threshold deliberately: this model chapter defines cases, separates subject and object, builds each noun/article form actually used, explains names and pronouns, treats the two plot contrasts and distinguishes time/direction accusatives. Every cited example is translated; no reference-only paradigm cells.

Answer-key pass: closed tasks require one word, show cues before the attempt, preserve accents, and enumerate the indefinite/definite variants where both fit. B uses printed forms, not a second inflection test. Every bank is checked by substitution; first letters separate einn from enginn and repeated s-initial words. C is present-tense self-check, with two models, English rubrics, one Af hverju and En þú last. Closed Skrifaðu is the final section’s second exercise.
